lesson_title: The CPU and Von Neumann Architecture

findings.claim: The design that almost every modern CPU is built on was described by mathematician John von Neumann in 1945.
findings.notes: The First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC was distributed June 30, 1945. Von Neumann is correctly described as a mathematician.

findings.claim: Amdahl's Law: if 50% of a program must run sequentially, the maximum possible speedup from adding more cores is 2x — no matter how many cores you add.
findings.notes: Amdahl's Law formulated by Gene Amdahl in 1967. The 2x maximum speedup for 50% sequential fraction is mathematically correct: S = 1/(0.5 + 0.5/∞) = 2.

findings.claim: CDs hold around 700 MB, DVDs 4.7 GB (or 8.5 GB dual-layer) and Blu-ray discs up to 50 GB.
findings.notes: Standard capacity figures are accurate. Single-layer Blu-ray is 25 GB, dual-layer 50 GB — the '50 GB' figure correctly refers to dual-layer.

lesson_title: Signed Binary, Addition, Subtraction and Shifts

findings.claim: Every mainstream CPU since the 1970s has used two's complement for signed integer storage.
findings.notes: Two's complement has been universal in mainstream CPU architectures since the early 1970s. The claim is accurate.

findings.claim: ASCII was developed in the 1960s and became the dominant early standard. Standard ASCII uses 7 bits per character, giving 2^7 = 128 possible codes (0 to 127).
findings.notes: ASCII approved as a standard on June 17, 1963. 7-bit encoding giving 128 codes is correct.

findings.claim: Upper-case letters A–Z (codes 65–90), Lower-case letters a–z (codes 97–122), Digits 0–9 (codes 48–57).
findings.notes: These ASCII code values are standard and correct.

findings.claim: Unicode currently defines over 140,000 characters (and the range can extend to over 1 million).
findings.notes: Unicode 15.1 defines 149,813 characters; the codespace extends to 1,114,112 code points.

lesson_title: Graphics: Pixels, Resolution and Colour Depth
notes: 24-bit = 16,777,216 colours (2^24) is correct. Bitmap formula, worked examples, and colour depth descriptions are accurate.

findings.claim: A sample rate of 44,100 Hz (44.1 kHz) means 44,100 measurements are recorded every second — this is the standard for CD-quality audio.
findings.notes: CD audio (Red Book standard) uses 44,100 Hz sample rate and 16-bit depth. This is accurate.

findings.claim: The Nyquist theorem states that a sample rate of at least twice the highest frequency is needed to reproduce it.
findings.notes: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem is correctly described.

findings.claim: De Morgan's laws describe how to distribute a NOT across an AND or OR. First law: NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B. Second law: NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.
findings.notes: De Morgan's laws are correctly stated.

lesson_title: Ethical, Cultural, Environmental and Privacy Impacts
notes: Data centres ~1% global electricity consumption is a widely cited estimate consistent with published research. No specific Acts, named inventors, or attributed algorithms. Claims are general/contextual.

findings.claim: Unauthorised access to computer material — hacking into a system you are not permitted to use, even if no data is taken. This is a summary offence, punishable by up to 2 years in prison.
findings.notes: Section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 is an EITHER-WAY offence, not a summary offence. The 2-year maximum applies on INDICTMENT (Crown Court trial), not on summary conviction. On summary conviction the maximum is 12 months. The Police and Justice Act 2006 made s.1 triable either way. Calling it 'a summary offence' and attaching the indictment-level penalty to it conflates two different trial modes and could cause students to misstate the law in an exam.
findings.fix: Replace 'This is a summary offence, punishable by up to 2 years in prison.' with 'This is an either-way offence: tried in a Magistrates' Court (summary conviction) it carries up to 12 months' imprisonment; tried in the Crown Court (on indictment) it carries up to 2 years' imprisonment.'

findings.claim: RIPA was later supplemented by the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 (sometimes called the 'Snoopers' Charter'), which updated and extended the framework for bulk data collection and equipment interference by intelligence services.
findings.notes: The IPA 2016 did not merely 'supplement' RIPA 2000 — it substantially repealed and replaced RIPA's interception and communications data acquisition provisions. The word 'supplemented' understates the replacement. Significant portions of RIPA (covert surveillance, CHIS) do remain in force, so it was a partial rather than total replacement, but 'supplemented' is misleading for students. The IPA 2016 is the primary legislation now.
findings.fix: Replace 'supplemented by' with 'largely replaced by (for interception and communications data) — though parts of RIPA relating to covert surveillance remain in force'.

findings.claim: Computer Misuse Act 1990, Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, Data Protection Act 2018 (UK GDPR), Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA), Freedom of Information Act 2000.
findings.notes: All five Act names and years are accurate.

findings.claim: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects creators' intellectual property automatically from the moment a work is created — no registration is required.
findings.notes: UK copyright arises automatically on creation without registration. This is accurate.

findings.claim: The FOI Act: the public body must respond within 20 working days.
findings.notes: Section 10(1) FOIA 2000 requires response within 20 working days of receipt.
